vignette: Mira, a 32-year-old single woman of South Asian descent, is a dedicated city council member who has always been passionate about community development and public safety. Her life took an unexpected turn two years ago when she was in the middle of a man-made disaster that left her shaken to her core. It happened on a crisp autumn evening as Mira was returning home from a late meeting at City Hall. She had just entered her apartment building when a loud explosion rocked the neighborhood, causing panic and chaos everywhere. The sound came from nearby where a gas pipeline had been negligently damaged during construction work, leading to a massive blast that devastated several buildings and claimed lives. Mira was unharmed but traumatized by what she witnessed in the aftermath. She watched as firefighters battled raging flames, emergency medical technicians rushed to assist victims, and people ran frantically through the streets in disarray. The images of destruction and suffering are seared into her memory and often haunt her in nightmares where the noise and chaos never stop. Since that day, Mira has been struggling with intrusive memories and vivid flashbacks that often bring back the intense fear she felt during the explosion. She can still smell the burning debris and hear the screams of those caught up in the disaster. These experiences have left her feeling overwhelmed and anxious at times, particularly when there are loud noises or sudden movements around her. Mira's occupation as a city council member means that she is often required to speak in public forums and attend community meetings. However, the trauma has affected her ability to perform these duties without significant distress. She frequently feels hypervigilant, constantly scanning for signs of danger even when there isn't any apparent threat. This heightened state of alertness can be exhausting, making it difficult for her to focus on complex policy issues or engage in detailed discussions. The disaster has also impacted her relationships with colleagues and constituents. Mira finds herself becoming irritable more easily than before, often snapping at people who ask questions about the gas pipeline incident. Her once warm demeanor has been replaced by a guarded approach as she tries to protect herself from further emotional pain. She describes feeling detached from others, finding it hard to connect on an emotional level and experiencing moments where she feels numb or "out of sync" with her surroundings. This detachment extends to her personal life; Mira has grown increasingly isolated since the disaster, pushing away close friends who express concern about her wellbeing. Another symptom that plagues Mira is insomnia. She often finds herself wide awake in the middle of the night, plagued by vivid images from that fateful evening. Her mind replays scenes over and over again as she tries to make sense of what happened and why she was unable to prevent it. The lack of sleep exacerbates her irritability and makes it harder for her to cope with the stressors of her job. Despite these challenges, Mira remains committed to her role in improving public safety and infrastructure within the city. She believes that by working towards preventing such disasters in the future, she can find some sense of purpose amidst the chaos. However, she acknowledges that this work is often emotionally draining, requiring a lot more resilience than before. As time passes, Mira has started to recognize how much her trauma impacts her daily life and relationships. She finds herself wondering if anyone will ever truly understand what she's gone through and whether she can ever fully recover from the man-made disaster that changed everything for her.
